From Source to Sea

Every river in the UK starts as rain falling on high ground, gathers into a channel, and flows downhill to the sea. Along the way it changes shape and behaviour. The upper course in the hills is steep and narrow; the middle course winds through gentler country; the lower course nears the sea is broad and flat. The journey of the River Severn or the Thames captures these changes in miniature — and the same processes shape every river worldwide.

Four Erosion Processes

A river wears away its bed and banks through four erosion processes. Hydraulic action: the sheer force of moving water pushes air into cracks, which eventually break apart. Abrasion (or corrasion): the river drags rocks and pebbles along, and these scour the bed and banks. Attrition: rocks crash into one another and break into smaller, rounder fragments. Solution (or corrosion): rivers flowing through limestone or chalk dissolve the rock chemically.

Key Fact

The four river erosion processes are hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution. Vertical erosion dominates the upper course; lateral erosion dominates the middle and lower courses.

Transport and Deposition

A river carries its load in four ways. Traction: large rocks roll along the bed. Saltation: smaller pebbles bounce. Suspension: fine clay and silt are carried in the water column, giving rivers their muddy colour. Solution: dissolved minerals travel invisibly. Deposition happens when the river loses energy — on the inside of meander bends, on flat floodplains, or where the river enters a lake or the sea.

Upper Course Landforms

In the steep upper course, vertical erosion dominates. Rivers cut downwards into the bedrock, creating V-shaped valleys with interlocking spurs (the river weaves between projecting hills). Where a band of hard rock sits above softer rock, a waterfall forms: water drops over the resistant lip, eroding a plunge pool below; the soft rock beneath undercuts, and the lip eventually collapses, retreating upstream. High Force on the River Tees in Co. Durham is a classic example. As waterfalls retreat, they leave a steep-sided gorge.

Middle Course Landforms

In the middle course, gradient eases and lateral erosion takes over. The river starts to swing from side to side, forming meanders. On the outside of a bend, fast-flowing water erodes a steep river cliff. On the inside, slower water deposits sand and gravel as a slip-off slope. Over time the loops widen until adjacent meanders meet during a flood; the river takes the shorter route and abandons the loop. The cut-off, banana-shaped lake left behind is an ox-bow lake.

Key Fact

Meanders form because flow is faster on the outside of bends (eroding) and slower on the inside (depositing). When two meanders meet, the river takes the shorter path and leaves an ox-bow lake.

Lower Course Landforms

Near the sea, the river is wide, deep and slow. Floodplains form on either side: when the river floods, it spreads out, slows down and deposits silt, building up flat fertile land. Levees are natural or built-up banks of coarser sediment that the river drops at its edges during floods, slightly raising the channel above the surrounding plain. At the sea, where the river drops the rest of its load, a delta can form — a fan of sediment criss-crossed with channels (the Nile and the Mississippi are classic deltas).

A storm hydrograph shows river discharge against time during and after a rain event. Bars show rainfall; a curve shows discharge. Lag time is the gap between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Short lag times (after heavy rain on impermeable ground) mean rapid runoff and risk of flash floods. Long lag times (after rain on porous chalk soils, or in heavily wooded catchments) are safer because water is delayed by infiltration. Urbanisation cuts lag time sharply because tarmac and concrete prevent infiltration.

On a 1:25,000 OS map, look for: tightly packed contour lines and a wiggling thin blue line (V-shaped valley, upper course); a sweeping blue line with light-coloured riverbank symbols and the word ‘Floodplain’ (middle/lower course); curved blue lines disconnected from the main river (ox-bow lakes); broad estuary mouths with mudflats marked. Examiners may give you an OS extract and ask you to identify which course of a river is shown — reading the contour spacing is the quickest clue.

This lesson covers the general fieldwork skills, terminology, and exam-paper expectations that apply to every student. The specific sites, data, and methods your class actually used will be different — for the case study you’ll write about in the exam, refer to your teacher’s notes and the data you collected on the day.

Geography You Can Touch

Fieldwork is what makes geography real. Reading about coastal erosion is one thing; actually measuring beach pebble shape, plotting wave fetch and explaining why one bay is wider than another is something else. The Edexcel B course requires every student to carry out two pieces of fieldwork — one in a physical environment (river or coast) and one in a human environment (urban or rural). The exam doesn’t test the result; it tests whether you understand the enquiry process.

The Six-Stage Enquiry Process

Edexcel sets out six stages and you need to know them in order. Stage 1: Formulating questions and hypotheses. A good enquiry question is specific and measurable: not ‘Is the river polluted?’ but ‘Does dissolved oxygen decline downstream of the weir?’. Stage 2: Selecting techniques and methods. Decide what to measure, how to measure it, and how often. Stage 3: Processing and presenting data. Choose appropriate graphs, maps and statistics. Stage 4: Analysis and explanation. Apply geographical theory to your findings. Stage 5: Drawing conclusions. State whether the hypothesis was supported by the evidence. Stage 6: Critical reflection. Evaluate accuracy, sample size, and what you would do differently.

Key Fact

The six enquiry stages run in order: questions, methods, presenting, analysis, conclusions, reflection. Examiners can ask about ANY two stages on any paper, so all six need to be solid.

Primary and Secondary Data

Primary data is what you collect yourself: pebble measurements at a beach, traffic counts in a town centre, questionnaires of residents. It’s tailored to your question. Secondary data is collected by someone else: census figures, Environment Agency flood maps, historical photographs, BGS geology maps. It’s already there but may not match your question exactly. Most enquiries combine both — primary data answers your specific question; secondary data sets the wider context.

Sampling: Why and How

You can’t measure every pebble on a beach or interview every resident. Sampling picks a manageable subset that represents the whole. Three main techniques: random sampling uses random numbers to choose locations — statistically unbiased but may miss important areas. Systematic sampling measures at fixed intervals (e.g. every 10 metres along a transect) — easy to plan, gives even coverage. Stratified sampling deliberately samples each subgroup (e.g. equal numbers from each ethnic group, age bracket or land-use type) — ensures every part of the population is represented.

Before any fieldwork, students must complete a risk assessment. Identify hazards (slippery rocks, traffic, cold water, deep mud, lone working in unfamiliar towns), rate the risk (low/medium/high) and list controls (work in pairs, keep below high-water mark, wear hi-vis, mobile phone). Naming the risk assessment when you evaluate your fieldwork shows professional conduct.

Presenting Data

Match the presentation method to the data type. Continuous data over time (river discharge, temperature) suit line graphs. Comparing categories (different beaches’ pebble sizes) suit bar charts. Showing patterns over space suit thematic maps (choropleth, isoline, proportional symbols, flow lines). Paired data suit scatter graphs with a line of best fit. Combine maps with photographs and field sketches for a richer presentation. Examiners often give students a graph and ask them to suggest an alternative method — have a clear answer ready.

Key Fact

Random sampling is unbiased; systematic sampling gives even coverage; stratified sampling ensures every subgroup is represented. Most fieldwork uses a mix.

Analysis, Conclusions and Reflection

Analysis links your findings to wider geographical theory. If pebbles are smaller and rounder downstream, you can refer to attrition. If a town centre has lower environmental quality scores than the suburbs, you can refer to housing markets and accessibility. Conclusions answer the original question with a clear ‘yes/no/partly’ based on the evidence. Reflection — the most-overlooked stage — is where you evaluate accuracy, sample size, possible bias and what you’d change. Strong reflections suggest specific improvements: ‘more sampling sites between sites 3 and 4 would have captured the change in gradient’ or ‘questionnaires only at 11 a.m. missed working residents’.

For your physical environment, choose between investigating coastal change/conflict or river processes/pressures. Possible questions: ‘How effective are sea defences at Hornsea?’; ‘Does river discharge increase downstream on the River Holme?’. For your human environment, choose between dynamic urban areas or changing rural areas. Possible questions: ‘How does environmental quality vary across Birmingham’s wards?’; ‘Why do rural deprivation indices vary across Cumbria?’. Each requires at least one quantitative method and one qualitative method.
